title: Antigravity Orchestrator: 1 Task, 2 Gemini Models Take Turns
description:
Antigravity Orchestrator explained in 60 seconds: since November 12, 2026, Orchestrator in Google Antigravity pairs 2 models in one task (by default 2 Gemini models): a planner model (Gemini 4 Carbon at launch and in Gemini Enterprise; on Google AI Pro and Ultra the default planner is now Gemini 4 Neon) explores the code, writes the plan and reviews the work, and the faster executor, Gemini 4 Hydrogen, makes the edits and runs the tests.
When the executor hits friction (for example a verification step that fails twice), it hands control back and the planner repairs the plan. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Google reports that Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. Our 10-step example (Carbon doing 2 steps instead of 10) is ours, not Google's.

Announcement: https://antigravity.google/blog/gemini-4-hydrogen-in-google-antigravity

Our example (invented, not a rate or a statistic): one coding task in 10 steps, a wall of 10 bricks. Before, one model does the whole task, so in our example Gemini 4 Carbon does all 10 steps; Google says that for everyday feature work and debugging inside a single session, running a frontier reasoning model with multiple parallel agents on every step of every routine task slows down your loop and burns frontier quota. Or you send the whole task to one cheaper model: Google says a static model router that sends the entire task to the cheapest model that is good enough starts breaking down as agents become longer running.
Now, in Google's example, Carbon reads the code and writes the plan and the faster Gemini 4 Hydrogen makes the edits and runs the tests; if, say, a check fails twice, Hydrogen hands back and Carbon repairs the plan: in our example Carbon does 2 steps, not 10.

Google's result: on Terminal-Bench 4.1, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. Google publishes no exact success rate or quota per step, so the 24% is for the whole run, not for 2 of our 10 steps.

How it works, from Google's docs: Orchestrator is not a router that classifies your prompt upfront and sends the whole request to a single model; both models collaborate within the same task and hand control back and forth as the work unfolds, automatically within a single response. Each message you send starts with a read-only planning phase in which the planner explores the codebase, resolves ambiguities, and writes a concrete implementation plan.
The executor hands control back when it runs into friction, such as a verification step that fails twice, an interface that behaves differently than expected, or a design choice the plan didn't settle. On longer tasks, and whenever you send a message while the executor is working, the executor reports its progress to the planner, which checks what was done against the plan and then wraps up the completed task, continues the remaining steps, or updates the plan.

Who can use it and what you can pick: Orchestrator is available for Google AI Ultra and Google AI Pro (paid plans, or trials with eligible premium devices), and in Gemini Enterprise. On Google AI Pro and Google AI Ultra you can choose the planner (Gemini 4 Neon, the default, Gemini 4 Carbon, Gemini 4 Argon or Claude Opus 5.5) and the executor (Gemini 4 Hydrogen, the default, or Claude Sonnet 5.5); in Gemini Enterprise, Orchestrator only runs Gemini 4 Carbon (High) as the planner with Gemini 4 Hydrogen (High) as the executor. Google calls Orchestrator the recommended default for most day-to-day development (feature work, bug fixes, refactoring, multi-file debugging) and points to a single model (Gemini 4 Neon, Carbon or Argon) for work where every intermediate step needs maximum reasoning depth.

A press caveat: InfoWorld (November 13, 2026) reports that Jena pointed out that Antigravity's documentation does not currently describe per-step logs identifying which model performed each action.

The wall and robots are our own drawing, not Google's.
